On Oct 29 the FTC and eight states sued a restaurant payments company. The complaint says a \$0 a month plan came with a higher processing fee, add-ons were billed without consent, and cancelling was made hard. The company denies it and says it will fight.

Whatever the court decides, it's a good weekend to pull out your own processor agreement and check four things.

1. Every fee on your statement has a name and a matching line in the contract. If a number doesn't match a line, ask what it is.

2. Who keeps the fees your customers pay at checkout. Some "online order" or convenience fees go to the provider, not to you.

3. What turned on without a signature. Add-ons, renewals, a plan change you don't remember agreeing to.

4. How you leave. The notice period, any termination fee, and whether your saved customer cards move with you.

The agencies say it's the first time the online subscription law (ROSCA) has been used against contracts between businesses. American Banker counts about 50 ROSCA cases so far.

Which line on your last statement could you not explain?

An insurance company's puppet mascot has 77 million YouTube views on its launch ad. A Facebook group with more than 40,000 members exists to hate it. Last weekend a YouTuber held a protest outside the company's Boston office.

The brand's own TikTok post on Oct 22 got 514 likes.

Their marketing chief says the engagement is the point. For an insurer everyone already knows, maybe it is.

For a store it isn't. Attention only turns into money on the page where someone pays, and November is when you find out how much of your attention makes it that far.

Can they pay the way they pay everywhere else, without typing a card number?

A cost that shows up on the last step is the most common reason people leave a cart: \[48%\] of US shoppers who abandoned one said extra costs like shipping, tax and fees were too high \[Baymard Institute\]. Put shipping on the product page or the cart, not at the end.

A payments company just put a merchant's payment data inside ChatGPT and Claude.

I like where this is going. I'd still ask four questions before connecting any payments account to an AI assistant:

1. What can it read? Orders, customer emails, payouts, card details.
2. Can it act, or only answer? A refund is an action. So is a cancelled subscription.
3. Where do the chats live, and who on your team can read them?
4. How do you switch it off in one click if something looks wrong?

If the answers fit on one page, connect it.
If nobody can answer number 2, wait a month.

Clocks go back at 2 a.m. this Sunday, Nov 1. In the US, the hour from 1 to 2 a.m. happens twice.

If a subscription renewal, a cart email or the end of your Halloween sale is scheduled in that hour, check it before Saturday.

From Nov 12, the Meta Pixel turns on a new setting by default: "Measure conversions on customer devices". It counts purchases matched on the shopper's phone that never reached your reports before (PPC Land, Oct 27).

In Meta's earlier test, advertisers saw about 3% more conversions on average.

So your ad report may show more purchases in Black Friday week. Your checkout won't take a single extra order because of it.

Before Nov 12, write down three numbers from the last 14 days:

1. Orders per day, from your store.
2. Checkout conversion rate: people who reached checkout and paid.
3. Purchases per day, as Meta reports them.

After Nov 12, compare the same three. If only the third one moves, look at the setting before you raise the budget.

You can turn it off per Pixel in Events Manager.

How big is the gap between Meta's number and your orders today?

The Visa and Mastercard swipe-fee settlement goes to a final approval hearing on Nov 16.

What it would change, per Payments Dive (Oct 16):
- Credit interchange down 10 basis points for five years.
- A 1.25% rate on standard consumer cards for eight years.
- The right to decline some premium and commercial credit cards.
- New rights to add surcharges or offer discounts, to steer customers toward cheaper cards.

For scale: merchants paid 2.35% on average on Visa and Mastercard transactions in 2024 (Nilson Report).

Walmart, the NRF and RILA have objected, so none of this is final yet.

One thing worth doing before the ruling: pull last month's orders and split them by card type. Standard, premium, commercial. That split tells you whether any of this moves the needle for your store.

\[If confirmed: where that card-type split lives in the TagadaPay dashboard.\]

Meta now lets you book an ad burst: your reach packed into a window of 3 to 24 hours (Ads Super Burst). It's also testing First Impression Ads in the US, the first ad slot in Feed, one brand per day.

Both sell the same thing. A lot of people at your checkout at the same time.

The ad dashboard stops at the tap. What happens after it is on you.

Before you book a window:
1. Place a test order on your phone, on mobile data, through the exact link the ad will use.
2. Count the fields between the cart and the pay button.
3. Try a card that declines. See what the customer sees, and whether there's another way to pay on the same page.
4. Check that your post-purchase offer loads after the payment, not before it.

Then book the window.

A breakfast sandwich ad from 2018 is one of the most-used sounds on TikTok this week. Nobody planned that. The ad was just good, and good ads keep working. If your best ad from last holiday season is sitting in an archive, run it again. Place one test order through it first. The ad held up. The product page it points to might not have.

DoorDash agreed to buy Instacart this week, for about $17 billion. Most of the takes are about delivery apps. The part that matters for a store is quieter. When someone buys your product through a marketplace, the marketplace keeps the customer. The email, the order history, the reorder button. All theirs. When someone buys through your own checkout, those stay with you.

nov 1. it's time. the store switched overnight. so did the checkout. the decor can wait. Feeds went from pumpkins to Christmas at midnight. If your store did too, check that the checkout made the switch: a place to write a gift note, and an order-by date someone can trust before they pay.
